items.prompt: What is the far side of the Moon?

options.label: The side that always faces the Sun
options.feedback: The far side does not always face the Sun; it faces away from Earth.

options.label: The hemisphere that faces away from Earth
options.feedback: That is correct: the far side is the half of the Moon that points away from our planet.

options.label: The side that is always in darkness
options.feedback: The far side receives sunlight like the near side; 'dark' here means unseen, not unlit.

options.label: The side that faces Earth during a new moon
options.feedback: That is the near side; the far side is always opposite Earth.

items.ok_line: Yes, the far side is the hemisphere pointing away from Earth.
items.ko_line: The far side is defined by its direction away from Earth, not by light or darkness.
items.exp_text: The far side of the Moon is the half that never faces Earth. Because the Moon is tidally locked, it always shows the same hemisphere to us, so the opposite hemisphere is called the far side. The name has nothing to do with sunlight.

items.prompt: Why is the far side of the Moon sometimes called the 'dark side'?

options.label: Because it is unseen from Earth, not because it lacks light
options.feedback: Exactly: 'dark' here means hidden from view, while both sides receive similar sunlight.

options.label: Because it never receives any sunlight
options.feedback: That is a common mistake; the far side gets as much sunlight as the near side on average.

options.label: Because it is always covered in shadow during lunar night
options.feedback: Lunar night affects both sides; the far side is not permanently dark.

options.label: Because it faces away from the Sun
options.feedback: The far side faces away from Earth, but it faces the Sun half of the month.

items.ok_line: Yes, 'dark' means unseen in this nickname.
items.ko_line: The far side is not in permanent darkness.
items.exp_text: People call the far side the dark side because it was never visible from Earth until spacecraft flew around it. The word 'dark' here means unknown or unseen, not lacking sunlight. Both hemispheres get roughly equal illumination from the Sun.

items.prompt: How much of the far side can occasionally be seen from Earth?

options.label: None of it
options.feedback: That is wrong: some crescent edges are visible due to a slight rocking motion called libration.

options.label: About half of it
options.feedback: Only a small fraction is visible; the rest stays hidden.

options.label: About 18% of it
options.feedback: Correct: libration lets us glimpse only about 18% of the far side from Earth.

options.label: All of it
options.feedback: The far side is never fully in view; the Moon always shows the same face.

items.ok_line: Yes, only about 18% ever peeks into view.
items.ko_line: Libration reveals a bit more than half of the whole Moon, but only a small part of the far side.
items.exp_text: The Moon's slight wobble in its orbit lets us see a little more than half of its total surface over time. Of the far side specifically, about 18% becomes visible at some point, while the remaining 82% stays unobservable from Earth.

items.prompt: How much of the far side's surface is covered by the dark, flat regions known as maria?

options.label: About 31%
options.feedback: That is the percentage on the near side, not the far side.

options.label: About half
options.feedback: The far side has relatively few maria, so this is too high.

options.label: About 10%
options.feedback: The actual figure is much lower, just 1%.

options.label: Only about 1%
options.feedback: Yes, the far side is almost entirely without the dark basalt plains.

items.ok_line: Correct: only 1% of the far side is maria.
items.ko_line: The near side has 31.2% maria, while the far side has just 1%.
items.exp_text: Maria are the dark, smooth plains formed by ancient lava flows. On the far side they cover only 1% of the surface, whereas the near side has 31.2% covered. This difference makes the far side appear brighter and more heavily cratered.

items.prompt: Where are the Moon's highest and lowest points located?

options.label: On the far side
options.feedback: Correct: the far side holds the most extreme elevations, including the tallest mountains measured from base to peak.

options.label: On the near side
options.feedback: The near side has gentler terrain; the extremes are all on the far side.

options.label: At the Moon's equator
options.feedback: Elevation extremes are not tied to the equator; they are on the far side.

options.label: At the poles
options.feedback: The highest and lowest points are not at the poles.

items.ok_line: Yes, the far side has the highest and lowest points.
items.ko_line: Both the highest and lowest elevations are found on the far side.
items.exp_text: The far side shows more dramatic changes in elevation than the near side. It contains the Moon's highest point, lowest point, and the tallest mountains measured from base to peak, making its landscape far more varied.

items.prompt: Which large crater or basin is found on the far side of the Moon?

options.label: Oceanus Procellarum
options.feedback: That is a large mare on the near side, not a crater on the far side.

options.label: Mare Orientale
options.feedback: Mare Orientale is a basin that can be glimpsed via libration, but it is not the largest crater mentioned on the far side.

options.label: The South Pole–Aitken basin
options.feedback: Yes, this is one of the largest craters in the Solar System, located on the far side.

options.label: The Apollo basin
options.feedback: That is a smaller basin on the far side, but the question asks for the largest one.

items.ok_line: Correct: South Pole–Aitken is a huge far-side crater.
items.ko_line: The largest mentioned on the far side is the South Pole–Aitken basin.
items.exp_text: The far side contains the South Pole–Aitken basin, one of the largest impact craters in the entire Solar System. It is a massive depression that dominates the southern part of the far side.

items.prompt: Why does the far side show so many more visible craters than the near side?

options.label: Because Earth shields it from impacts
options.feedback: Earth blocks only a tiny part of the sky, so it cannot shield the Moon.

options.label: Because it receives more impacts than the near side
options.feedback: Both sides receive roughly the same number of impacts.

options.label: Because the craters are older there
options.feedback: The key difference is that lava flows on the near side covered many craters, not age.

options.label: Because lava flows on the near side covered its craters
options.feedback: Yes, the near side's volcanic resurfacing hid many craters, while the far side kept them visible.

items.ok_line: Correct: near-side lava flows buried craters.
items.ko_line: Earth provides almost no shielding, and both sides get equal impacts.
items.exp_text: Both hemispheres of the Moon have received about the same number of impacts. However, the near side has extensive lava plains that flooded and obscured many old craters, while the far side has few such flows, so its craters remain visible.

items.prompt: What did the Chang'e 6 mission do on the far side of the Moon?

options.label: It collected samples and brought them back to Earth
options.feedback: Correct: it was the first sample-return mission from the far side.

options.label: It took the first photos of the far side
options.feedback: That was done by Luna 3 decades earlier.

options.label: It carried astronauts around the Moon
options.feedback: No astronauts were on this mission.

options.label: It built a radio telescope there
options.feedback: A radio telescope is only a suggestion, not something this mission did.

items.ok_line: Yes, Chang'e 6 brought far-side samples to Earth.
items.ko_line: It did not photograph, carry people, or build a telescope.
items.exp_text: The Chang'e 6 mission landed in the Apollo basin on the far side, collected rock and soil samples, and returned them to Earth in 2024. This was the first time any material from the far side was brought back for study.

items.prompt: What does the term 'dark side of the Moon' actually mean?

options.label: The side that never receives sunlight
options.feedback: That is a common misconception. Every part of the Moon gets about two weeks of sunlight followed by two weeks of night. 'Dark' here means unseen, not unlit.

options.label: The side that is never visible from Earth
options.feedback: Yes. Because the Moon is tidally locked, the far side never faces Earth, so it stayed unseen until spacecraft photographed it. It still gets sunlight like any other part.

options.label: The side that is always in shadow during a lunar eclipse
options.feedback: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, but that affects the near side, not the far side. The nickname refers to being unseen, not shadowed.

options.label: The side that is darker in color due to fewer bright craters
options.feedback: Actually, the far side has fewer dark maria and is more reflective, making it brighter overall. The 'dark' in the nickname is about visibility, not color.

items.ok_line: The far side is called dark because it was never seen from Earth, not because it lacks sunlight.
items.ko_line: Remember, 'dark side' refers to the far side being hidden from view, not to darkness.
items.exp_text: The far side of the Moon is sometimes called the dark side, but 'dark' there means unseen or unknown, not unilluminated. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same hemisphere always faces Earth, leaving the far side hidden until spacecraft visited it. Every location on the Moon experiences about two weeks of sunlight and two weeks of night, so the far side is not permanently dark.

items.prompt: Why does the far side of the Moon never fully come into view from Earth?

options.label: Because Earth blocks the view of that hemisphere
options.feedback: Earth does not block the view; the Moon itself rotates and orbits at the same rate, so the same face is always turned toward Earth. That is tidal locking.

options.label: Because the Moon spins faster than it orbits
options.feedback: That would make different parts of the Moon visible over time. Instead, the rotation period matches the orbital period, so the same side always faces Earth.

options.label: Because the Moon rotates once for every orbit it makes around Earth
options.feedback: Correct. Tidal locking means the Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period, so the far side never turns toward Earth. Only about 18% of it is glimpsed through libration.

options.label: Because the far side is too dark to be seen
options.feedback: The far side does receive sunlight. It is invisible from Earth because the Moon's rotation keeps that hemisphere turned away, not because it is dark.

items.ok_line: The Moon spins once per orbit, so the far side never faces Earth.
items.ko_line: The Moon's spin matches its orbit, keeping the far side hidden.
items.exp_text: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, meaning the time it takes to rotate once equals the time it takes to orbit Earth once. As a result, the same hemisphere always points toward Earth, so the far side never fully comes into view. Small wobbles called libration let us glimpse about 18% of the far side, but the rest is only visible from spacecraft.
